h1: Content writing cost in India, from ₹0.50 to ₹8 a word
metaTitle: Content Writing Cost in India: Per-Word Rates 2026
metaDescription: Content writing costs ₹0.50 to ₹8 per word in India. Here is what each rate buys, and why one article that can actually rank costs about ₹11,000 all in.
answer: Content writers in India charge ₹0.50 to ₹8 per word. But per-word is the wrong unit: a 1,500-word post at ₹2/word is ₹3,000 of drafting and roughly ₹11,000 by the time you've paid for the brief, the expert input, the edit, the images and the publishing. That's ₹7.33 a word, all in.
takeaways: The draft is usually **under a third** of what a publishable article costs. Everything expensive happens before and after the writing.
₹2 a word is plenty for cluster and comparison pages. ₹8 a word earns itself only where first-hand expertise is the ranking constraint.
AI cuts the drafting line by 60–80% and cuts **nothing else**. An ₹11,000 article becomes ₹8,500, not ₹1,000.
A ₹75,000 retainer honestly funds three to four new articles a month, or six to eight if half are refreshes of pages you already own.
Commission one paid trial article at full rate before you sign anything monthly.

body: Indian content pricing is unusually wide because the market spans two completely different products under one job title: text that fills a page, and text that a practitioner wrote. Both are quoted per word, which is the source of most of the confusion.

callout.title: The ₹0.50 trap
callout.body: At fifty paise a word, a 1,500-word article costs ₹750. It reads fine. It also says exactly what the four pages above it already said, which is the one thing Google's helpful-content systems are built to spot. You'll pay for it twice: once to publish, again to unpublish.

callout.title: The ratio to remember
callout.body: Drafting is 27% of the cost of a publishable article. When an agency quotes you "₹4,000 per blog", ask which of the other five lines they've dropped. Usually it's the expert input and the images — the two that make the page different from everyone else's.

sections.h2: AI first drafts: what they save now, what they cost later
body: A language model will produce a competent 1,500-word draft in two minutes. That collapses the ₹3,000 line to something between ₹300 and ₹1,200 of prompting and cleanup. Genuinely useful, and we use it.

It does not touch the other ₹8,000. The brief still needs a human who's read the SERP. The expert interview still needs a human who did the job. The edit gets *longer*, because reviewing fluent, confident, subtly wrong prose is slower than fixing a human's clumsy but honest sentence. Images still need making.

So the realistic saving is ₹11,000 down to roughly ₹8,500 — about 23%. Anyone selling you AI content at ₹500 an article has removed the eight thousand rupees that made it rank, not found an efficiency.

The deferred cost is the part that stings. Google's guidance has never been about production method; it's about whether the page is helpful and demonstrates first-hand experience. Publish two hundred undifferentiated pages and you get a site that dilutes its own internal link equity, spreads crawl attention thin, and eventually needs an expensive pruning exercise. We wrote about that at length in [does AI-written content still rank](/journal/does-ai-written-content-still-rank).

sections.h2: How many articles a ₹75,000 retainer actually funds
body: Content usually takes 40–50% of an SEO retainer. On ₹75,000/month that's ₹30,000–₹37,500 — three to four fully loaded new articles.

That number roughly doubles if half the programme is refreshes rather than new pages. Updating an existing article that already has links and history costs ₹4,000–₹6,000 and frequently outperforms a brand-new page, because you're adding to something Google already trusts rather than starting at zero.

callout.title: Cadence beats volume
callout.body: Four solid articles a month for twelve months beats fifty in one quarter and silence after. Search systems reward sites that stay alive; your competitors mostly won't.

sections.h2: When ₹8 a word earns it, and when ₹2 is plenty
body: Paying specialist rates for every page is how content budgets die in month five. Paying generalist rates for the pages that decide your credibility is how content programmes fail entirely. Split the list.

bullets: **YMYL categories** — health, finance, legal, insurance. Experience and expertise are the ranking constraint, and a generalist cannot fake either.
**B2B and SaaS**, where your reader does the job for a living and will spot a writer who doesn't within two paragraphs.
**Pillar pages** you expect to link to for three years. Amortised across that lifespan, the premium is rounding error.
**Anything a competitor already covers with a real practitioner's byline.** You can't out-volume expertise.
Definition and glossary pages, where the job is accuracy and completeness, not insight.
Supporting cluster articles that exist to catch long-tail queries and pass link equity upward.
Product and category descriptions, once someone has written the template properly.
Location pages — provided a human adds genuinely local detail, otherwise you've built scaled content.

sections.h2: Test a writer before you commit to a year of them
body: Commission one paid trial article at the full rate, on your hardest topic, with the exact brief you'd use ongoing. It costs ₹3,000–₹12,000 and it settles the question faster than any portfolio. Judge it on three things, none of which is prose quality.
numbered: **Did they ask questions before writing?** A writer who accepts a brief without a single clarifying question is about to produce something generic.

**Is there one fact in it that isn't on page one of Google?** A number from your CRM, a quote from your ops lead, a screenshot of your own dashboard. That fact is the whole reason the page can outrank an incumbent.
**Does the structure match what's ranking?** If the top five results are comparison tables and your writer filed nine paragraphs of prose, they researched the topic and not the search results.

faqs.q: What is the average content writing rate in India?
faqs.a: Most commercial work is commissioned between ₹1 and ₹4 per word. Below ₹1 you're in mill territory; above ₹5 you're paying for subject-matter expertise rather than writing. For a 1,500-word article that's ₹1,500 to ₹6,000 of drafting — before the brief, edit and images that make it publishable.

faqs.q: How much does one SEO blog post cost in India?
faqs.a: Around ₹11,000 fully loaded for a 1,500-word article — ₹3,000 of drafting plus ₹8,000 of brief, expert input, editing, images and publishing. Agencies quoting ₹4,000 a post have removed lines from that list; ask which ones before you decide it's a bargain.

faqs.q: Should I pay per word or per article?
faqs.a: Per article, with the deliverable defined. Per-word pricing quietly rewards length, and length is not a ranking factor — matching search intent is. A tight 900-word answer that satisfies the query beats a padded 2,400-word one, but only one of them is cheaper under a per-word contract.

faqs.q: Is AI-generated content cheaper for SEO?
faqs.a: It cuts the drafting cost by 60–80% and leaves the other 70% of the bill untouched. Editing often takes longer, because confident, fluent, wrong text is harder to review than clumsy honest text. Realistic saving on a publishable article: about 23%, not 90%.

faqs.q: How many blog posts a month do I need?
faqs.a: Fewer, better, consistently. Three to four fully researched articles a month — what a ₹75,000 retainer funds — sustained for a year, beats twenty thin posts a month for three months. Consistency also matters more than volume for topics where competitors publish sporadically.
